title: Microscopes: Seeing the Invisible
summary: How microscopes use lenses to magnify tiny things, how Robert Hooke named cells and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek first saw bacteria, and how doctors and scientists use microscopes today.
poll: The microscope is one of the most important tools ever invented.

versions.title: Seeing Small Things
versions.text:
Look at a drop of pond water. It looks clear. But it is full of life! The life in it is too small to see.

A microscope can help. It has a lens. A lens is a bit of glass. It has a curve. It bends light. Then small things look big. That is how it can magnify things.

Robert Hooke used one long ago. He looked at a thin slice of cork. He saw lots of small boxes. He called them cells. Now we know this. All things that live are made of cells. You are made of cells, too!

A man in Holland sold cloth. He made his own small lens. His name was Antonie van Leeuwenhoek. He looked at a drop of water. He saw small things swim! No one had seen them yet.

Some small things are germs. Germs can make us sick. Doctors look for them. They use a microscope. Then they know what is wrong.

Some new ones do not use light. They make things look a million times as big!

versions.title: Microscopes: Seeing Tiny Things

versions.title: Microscopes: Seeing the Invisible
versions.text:
Scoop up a single drop of water from a pond, and it will probably look clear and empty. In fact, it may hold thousands of tiny organisms, or living things. They are too small for our eyes to see.

To study this hidden world, scientists use a microscope. Every microscope has at least one lens, a curved piece of glass that bends light. Because the light bends, small objects look much bigger. When a lens makes an object look larger, we say it can magnify it. The object being studied is called a specimen. It is usually placed on a thin glass slide.

About 350 years ago, the English scientist Robert Hooke examined a thin slice of cork. He saw rows of tiny empty boxes and named them cells. Today we know that all living things are made of cells.

At about the same time, a Dutch cloth seller named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was grinding his own tiny lenses. When he looked at drops of water, he saw little creatures darting about. These included bacteria, and he was the first person to see them.

Some bacteria are germs that cause sickness. Doctors use a microscope to look for them in blood. Most school microscopes use two lenses and can magnify about 400 times. Newer microscopes use electrons instead of light and can magnify more than a million times.

versions.title: Microscopes: Seeing the Invisible
versions.text:
If you collect a single drop of water from a pond, it will probably appear transparent and empty. In reality, it may contain thousands of living organisms that are simply too small for unaided human eyes to detect, and for most of history nobody even suspected that they existed.

To investigate this hidden world, scientists depend on an instrument called the microscope. Every microscope contains at least one lens, a curved piece of transparent glass that bends light as it passes through. Because the light bends, a tiny object appears considerably larger than it actually is, and the amount by which it is enlarged is called its magnification. The object being examined is called a specimen, and it is usually positioned on a thin glass slide.

Approximately 350 years ago, the English scientist Robert Hooke examined a thin slice of cork through his microscope. He observed rows of tiny empty compartments, which he named cells because they reminded him of small rooms. Scientists now understand that every living organism is constructed from cells.

During the same period, a Dutch cloth merchant named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was patiently grinding his own miniature lenses. Although his instruments contained only a single lens, they were remarkably powerful. When he examined drops of water, he discovered little creatures darting energetically about. Among them were bacteria, and he became the first person ever to observe them.

Because certain bacteria are germs that cause disease, doctors rely on microscopes to identify them in samples of blood. A typical school microscope is a compound microscope, which combines two lenses and reaches a magnification of approximately 400 times. Modern electron microscopes, which were developed in the 1930s, use beams of electrons instead of light, and they can achieve a magnification of more than a million times.

Microscopes have also become essential in many other fields. Entomologists, the scientists who study insects, use them to examine delicate wings and legs, while workers at water treatment plants use them to confirm that drinking water is free of harmful organisms. In Saudi classrooms, students use microscopes during science lessons to inspect onion skin, leaves, and grains of desert sand.

versions.title: Microscopes: Seeing the Invisible
versions.text:
If you collect a single drop of water from a pond, it will probably appear transparent and lifeless. In reality, it may contain thousands of living organisms that are far too small for unaided human eyes to detect, and throughout most of human history nobody even suspected that such creatures existed.

To investigate this concealed world, scientists depend on an instrument called the microscope. Every microscope contains at least one lens, a curved piece of transparent glass that bends light as it passes through. Because the light is refracted in this way, a minute object appears considerably larger than it actually is, and the degree to which it is enlarged is known as its magnification. The object under examination is called a specimen, and it is ordinarily positioned on a thin rectangular slide of glass, sometimes after being colored with a special dye that makes its structures easier to distinguish.

Approximately 350 years ago, the English scientist Robert Hooke examined a delicate slice of cork through his microscope. He observed orderly rows of tiny empty compartments, which he named cells because they reminded him of the small rooms in which monks lived. Biologists now understand that every living organism, from the humblest weed to the enormous blue whale, is constructed from cells.

During the same period, a Dutch cloth merchant named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was patiently grinding his own miniature lenses. Although his instruments contained only a single lens, they were remarkably powerful. When he examined droplets of water, he discovered microscopic creatures darting energetically about, and among them were bacteria, which no human being had ever previously observed.

Because certain bacteria are germs responsible for serious illnesses, physicians rely on microscopes to identify them in samples of blood. A typical classroom instrument is a compound microscope, which combines two lenses and reaches a magnification of approximately 400 times. Electron microscopes, which were developed during the 1930s, employ beams of electrons instead of light, and they can achieve a magnification exceeding a million times.

Beyond medicine, microscopes have become indispensable in numerous other fields. Entomologists, the scientists who specialize in insects, use them to examine delicate wings and antennae, while technicians at water treatment facilities rely on them to confirm that drinking water is free of harmful organisms. Even in Saudi classrooms, students operate microscopes during science lessons, systematically inspecting onion skin, leaf surfaces, and individual grains of desert sand that, under sufficient magnification, resemble polished, irregularly shaped jewels.

versions.title: Microscopes: Seeing the Invisible
versions.text:
If you were to collect a single drop of water from a pond, it would probably appear transparent and lifeless. In reality, it may contain thousands of living organisms that are far too minute for unaided human eyes to detect, and throughout most of human history nobody even suspected that such creatures existed.

To investigate this concealed world, scientists depend on an instrument called the microscope. Every microscope incorporates at least one lens, a precisely curved piece of transparent glass that bends light as it passes through. Because the light is refracted in this manner, a minute object appears considerably larger than it actually is, and the degree to which it is enlarged is known as its magnification. The object under examination is called a specimen, and it is ordinarily positioned on a thin rectangular slide of glass, occasionally after being treated with a special dye that makes its internal structures easier to distinguish.

Approximately 350 years ago, the English scientist Robert Hooke examined a delicate slice of cork through his microscope. He observed orderly rows of tiny empty compartments, which he named cells because they reminded him of the small, plain rooms in which monks lived. Biologists now recognize that every living organism, from the humblest desert weed to the enormous blue whale, is fundamentally constructed from cells.

During that same period, a Dutch cloth merchant named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was patiently grinding his own miniature lenses. Although his instruments contained only a single lens, they were extraordinarily powerful for their era. When he examined droplets of water, he discovered microscopic creatures darting energetically about, and among them were bacteria, which no human being had ever previously observed.

Because certain bacteria are germs responsible for serious illnesses, physicians rely on microscopes to identify them in samples of blood. A typical classroom instrument is a compound microscope, which combines two lenses and reaches a magnification of approximately 400 times. Electron microscopes, which were developed during the 1930s, employ concentrated beams of electrons instead of light, and they can achieve a magnification exceeding a million times, revealing even individual viruses.

Beyond medicine, microscopes have become indispensable in numerous other disciplines. Entomologists, the scientists who specialize in insects, use them to investigate the intricate architecture of wings and antennae, while technicians at water treatment facilities depend on them to confirm that drinking water is uncontaminated by harmful microorganisms. Even in Saudi classrooms, students operate microscopes during science lessons, systematically inspecting onion skin, leaf surfaces, and individual grains of desert sand that, under sufficient magnification, resemble polished, irregularly shaped gemstones, demonstrating that ordinary materials often conceal astonishing complexity.

MID.modelAnswer: Before microscopes, people had no idea that tiny living things existed in a single drop of water. Because of these discoveries, scientists learned that living things are built from cells and that whole worlds of tiny organisms exist all around us.

HIGH.prompt: Was Leeuwenhoek's discovery of bacteria or Hooke's discovery of cells more important? Make a claim and support it with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported my claim with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained my reasoning and used correct grammar and punctuation.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I believe Hooke's discovery of cells was more important because it revealed the basic unit that makes up every living organism, a foundation that the rest of biology still rests on. Hooke was the first to examine a specimen of cork and notice the tiny compartments he named cells, and scientists later learned that even the bacteria Leeuwenhoek found are themselves made of a single cell. Leeuwenhoek's work was remarkable because it showed that living organisms too small to see could cause illness, but understanding what those organisms actually were still depended on Hooke's idea of the cell. For that reason, Hooke's breakthrough provided the broader concept on which later microscopic science, including today's compound and electron microscopes, was built.
